title: Language Implementation vs. Language Features
summary: Programming Paradigms compared what languages let you SAY — OOP vs. functional vs. logic, as features you choose between. This discipline asks a different question: once a language exists on paper, how does a machine actually make a program written in it run?

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: Operational Semantics and Small-Step Evaluation
summary: Before building an interpreter, a language needs a precise, on-paper definition of what each expression actually evaluates to — small-step operational semantics gives exactly that, one inference rule at a time, on a language small enough to write every rule down in full.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 3-4 (Untyped Arithmetic Expressions)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: The Untyped Lambda Calculus
summary: Three constructs — a variable, a function, and a function call — turn out to be enough to build every programming language construct that exists; the lambda calculus is that minimal core, stripped of everything else so its evaluation rules can be studied directly.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 5 (The Untyped Lambda-Calculus)
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: Beta Reduction and Evaluation Strategies
summary: Beta reduction — substituting an argument for a bound variable — is the lambda calculus's one and only computation rule; the real design choice is WHEN to apply it, and call-by-value vs. call-by-name is that choice, made concrete on a term that behaves differently under each.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 5 (The Untyped Lambda-Calculus)
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: The Lambda Calculus as a Model of Computation

related.label: The Church-Turing Thesis and What "Computable" Means

summary: Church encodings show that booleans, numbers, and even recursion can be built from nothing but functions — real evidence for the Church-Turing thesis's claim that the lambda calculus, despite having no built-in data types at all, computes exactly what a Turing machine computes.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 5 (The Untyped Lambda-Calculus)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Lexical Analysis: Scanning Source into Tokens
summary: The first step from raw source text to a running program: a scanner walks the character stream once, left to right, and groups characters into tokens — numbers, identifiers, operators — the smallest units a parser is willing to work with.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 4 (Scanning)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Parsing Expressions into an Abstract Syntax Tree
summary: A parser takes the token stream and recovers its grammatical structure — literally applying the context-free grammar derivations already covered, but now building a tree instead of just deciding accept-or-reject.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 5-6 (Representing Code, Parsing Expressions)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Evaluating an AST: A Tree-Walking Interpreter
summary: An `eval` function that recurses over the AST, one node type at a time, is small-step operational semantics made runnable — every evaluation rule written on paper earlier becomes one case of a real function here.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 7 (Evaluating Expressions)
Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 4 (An ML Implementation of Arithmetic Expressions)

title: Environments and Variable Scope
summary: A variable name is not the value it holds — an environment is the runtime data structure (a chain of mappings) that actually connects the two, and lexical vs. dynamic scope is a real design choice about which environment a variable resolves against.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 8 (Statements and State)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Implementing Closures: The Environment That Outlives Its Frame
summary: Closures were already shown as a language FEATURE — a function that keeps working after its enclosing scope returns. Here is the implementation underneath: a function value is a pair of its code and the environment it was created in, kept alive by that pairing alone.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 10 (Functions)
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: Control Flow and Statements in an Interpreter
summary: An `if` or a `while` is not a special magic case for an interpreter — it is one more AST node type whose evaluation rule decides which of its children to evaluate, and how many times, entirely in terms of machinery already built.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 9 (Control Flow)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Functions and the Call Stack at Runtime
summary: The interpreter's own call stack (tree-walk recursion calling itself for a function call) and the real hardware call stack already covered are the same idea at two different levels: one frame per active call, torn down on return either way.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 10 (Functions)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Static vs. Dynamic Typing
summary: A static type system rejects some programs before they ever run; a dynamic one only discovers a type error the moment it happens at runtime — the same tradeoff (caught early vs. more flexible) that shows up in every real language's design.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 1 (Introduction)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Type Checking: Progress and Preservation
summary: "Well-typed programs don't go wrong" is not a slogan — it is exactly two provable properties: progress (a well-typed term is either done or can still take a step) and preservation (taking a step never changes a term's type).

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 8-9 (Typed Arithmetic Expressions, Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus)
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: The Simply Typed Lambda Calculus
summary: Adding one typing rule per lambda-calculus construct turns the untyped calculus into a small, real type system — a typing judgment written directly under a function, checked against a context, exactly like the progress/preservation properties it's designed to satisfy.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 9 (Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus)
Stanford CS242 — Programming Languages

title: Type Inference and the Need for Unification
summary: Writing every type annotation by hand gets tedious fast — type inference recovers the same typing judgments without them, by generating constraints between unknown types and solving those constraints by unification.

references.label: Pierce — Types and Programming Languages, Ch. 22 (Type Reconstruction)
ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area

title: Automatic Memory Management: Reference Counting and Tracing GC

related.label: Common Memory Bugs: Leaks and Dangling Pointers

summary: Manual heap management already showed exactly how a leak or a dangling pointer happens — a language runtime with automatic memory management exists specifically to make that entire bug class structurally impossible, at the cost of runtime work a C program never pays.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Programming Languages Knowledge Area
Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Ch. 26 (Garbage Collection)

title: Capstone: Assembling a Complete Tree-Walking Interpreter
summary: Every piece built in this discipline — scanner, parser, AST, environment, closures, control flow, a type checker — wired together into one small, working interpreter, mirroring how the CPU discipline's own capstone assembled gates and a datapath into a working machine.

references.label: Nystrom — Crafting Interpreters, Part II (A Tree-Walk Interpreter)
